title: Are these three statements about averages always true?
description: A question from the book gives three statements about the average of two even numbers, of two multiples of five, and of five multiples of five. The video writes each kind of number with a letter, finds the average with algebra, and checks each statement with numbers.
teaching_notes: One idea: write each number as a multiple times a letter, find the average, and see whether it keeps the property. Watch for students who test one example that works and call the statement true.

source: Figure it Out (more on mean and median, question 5)
video_script.why: The child cannot settle an always-true claim by trying a few numbers, so the video writes the numbers with letters and finds the average.
video_script.substitution: Write each number as a multiple times a letter, find the average with the letters, and check with numbers.
video_script.anchor: three statement cards about averages, each with a question mark
hold_back: Answer: All three statements are false
never_show: the word false for any statement before its check
maths_rules: (i) two even numbers 2a and 2b: average = (2a + 2b) / 2 = a + b, which can be odd; 2 and 4 give 3
(ii) two multiples of 5, 5a and 5b: average = 5(a + b) / 2, not always a multiple of 5; 5 and 10 give 7.5
(iii) five multiples of 5: average = (5a + 5b + 5c + 5d + 5e) / 5 = a + b + c + d + e, which need not be a multiple of 5; 5, 5, 5, 5, 10 give 30 / 5 = 6
each statement fails once, so all three are false
video_script.design: One idea: letters find the average of any numbers of the kind. The three statement cards stay from ground to the end of the idea part.

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about three statements on averages.
<bookmark mark='cards'/>One says the average of two even numbers is even.
<bookmark mark='second'/>Another says the average of two multiples of five is a multiple of five. The third says the same for five multiples of five.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Is each statement always true?

beats.on_screen: the three statement cards and the question marks stay; Keeko sits at the corner of the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board while the cards stay in view

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: an even number is written 2 × a letter; a multiple of 5 is written 5 × a letter

marks.even: an even number is written as 2 times a letter, such as 2a
marks.five: a multiple of 5 is written as 5 times a letter, such as 5a

narration: <bookmark mark='even'/>We use the same way as the example in your book. Any even number is two times a whole number, written two eigh.
<bookmark mark='five'/>Any multiple of five is five times a whole number, written five eigh.

beats.on_screen: Given: three statements about the average of even numbers and multiples of 5

marks.given: the three statements are written as the given

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, three statements about the average of even numbers and of multiples of five.

beats.on_screen: To find: whether each statement is always true, and why

marks.find: the thing to find is written under the given

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to decide whether each statement is always true, and give a reason.

beats.on_screen: two even numbers 2a and 2b: average = (2a + 2b) ÷ 2 = a + b, which can be odd

marks.write: the two even numbers are written as 2a and 2b
marks.avg: (2a + 2b) ÷ 2 = a + b is written, with a note: can be odd

narration: <bookmark mark='write'/>Step one, the two even numbers. Write them as two eigh and two bee.
<bookmark mark='avg'/>Their average is two eigh plus two bee, divided by two, which is eigh plus bee. This can be odd.

beats.on_screen: two multiples of 5: 5a and 5b; average = 5(a + b) ÷ 2, not always a multiple of 5

marks.write: the two multiples of 5 are written as 5a and 5b
marks.avg: 5(a + b) ÷ 2 is written, with a note: not always a multiple of 5

narration: <bookmark mark='write'/>Step two, two multiples of five. Write them as five eigh and five bee.
<bookmark mark='avg'/>Their average is five times the sum of eigh and bee, all divided by two. Dividing by two does not always leave a multiple of five.

beats.on_screen: five multiples of 5: 5a, 5b, 5c, 5d, 5e; average = a + b + c + d + e, which need not be a multiple of 5

marks.write: the five multiples of 5 are written as 5a, 5b, 5c, 5d and 5e
marks.avg: (5a + 5b + 5c + 5d + 5e) ÷ 5 = a + b + c + d + e is written, with a note: need not be a multiple of 5

narration: <bookmark mark='write'/>Step three, five multiples of five. Write them as five eigh, five bee, five see, five dee and five ee.
<bookmark mark='avg'/>Their total divided by five is eigh plus bee plus see plus dee plus ee. This need not be a multiple of five.

beats.on_screen: check: 2 and 4 have average 3; 5 and 10 have average 7.5; 5, 5, 5, 5, 10 have average 30 ÷ 5 = 6

marks.two: 2 and 4 are written with their average 3, which is odd
marks.five: 5 and 10 are written with their average 7.5

narration: <bookmark mark='two'/>Step four, check with numbers. Two and four are even, but their average is three, which is odd.
<bookmark mark='five'/>Five and ten are multiples of five, but their average is seven point five.
<bookmark mark='fives'/>Five, five, five, five and ten add to thirty. Thirty divided by five is six, not a multiple of five.

beats.on_screen: Answer: All three statements are false

marks.ans: the answer line is boxed and each statement card is crossed out

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>All three statements are false.
One number that breaks a statement is enough to show it is not always true.
